questions.knowledge_point: Finding a Quadratic Taylor Polynomial in Matrix Form
questions.problem:
For the function $f:{R}^{2}\to R,$ defined as

$$
f(x,y)={x}^{2}+{e}^{x-y},
$$

the quadratic Taylor polynomial of $f$ about $a=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]$ is given by

$$
f(x,y)≈f(a)+{f}^{′}(a)(x-a)+\frac{1}{2}{[\begin{aligned}∗ \\ y-1\end{aligned}]}^{T}[\begin{aligned}3 & ∗ \\ -1 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}∗ \\ y-1\end{aligned}].
$$

Find the sum of the three missing expressions.
questions.worked_solution:
Suppose that the function $f:{R}^{n}\to R$ is defined by 

$$
f:[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2} \\ ⋮ \\ {x}_{n}\end{aligned}]⟶z
$$

 

and is twice differentiable at $x=a.$ Then, the quadratic Taylor polynomial of $f$ about $a$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & ≈f(a)+{f}^{′}(a)(x-a)+\frac{1}{2}(x-a)^{T}{f}^{″}(a)(x-a),\end{aligned}
$$

where

$$
{f}^{′}(a)={[\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂{x}_{1}} & \frac{∂f}{∂{x}_{2}} & ⋯ & \frac{∂f}{∂{x}_{n}}\end{aligned}]|}_{x=a}
$$

and

$$
{f}^{″}(a)={[\begin{aligned}\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{1}^{2}} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{1}∂{x}_{2}} & ⋯ & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{1}∂{x}_{n}} \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{2}∂{x}_{1}} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{2}^{2}} & ⋯ & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{2}∂{x}_{n}} \\ ⋮ & ⋮ & ⋮ & ⋮ \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{n}∂{x}_{1}} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{n}∂{x}_{2}} & ⋯ & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{n}^{2}}\end{aligned}]}_{x=a}
$$

In this case, we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(x) & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & \frac{∂f}{∂y}\end{aligned}], & \,{f}^{″}(x) & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂x∂y} \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂y∂x} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{y}^{2}}\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Calculating the first derivative, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(x) & =[\begin{aligned}2x+{e}^{x-y} & -{e}^{x-y}\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Calculating the second derivative, we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{″}(x) & =[\begin{aligned}2+{e}^{x-y} & -{e}^{x-y} \\ -{e}^{x-y} & {e}^{x-y}\end{aligned}] \\ {f}^{″}(1,1) & =[\begin{aligned}3 & -1 \\ -1 & 1\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the second-degree Taylor polynomial is given by

$$
f(x)≈f(a)+{f}^{′}(a)(x-a)+\frac{1}{2}{[\begin{aligned}x-1 \\ y-1\end{aligned}]}^{T}[\begin{aligned}3 & -1 \\ -1 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}x-1 \\ y-1\end{aligned}].
$$

Finally, the sum of the missing expressions is

$$
(x-1)+(-1)+(x-1)=2x-3.
$$

questions.problem:
For the function $f:{R}^{2}\to R,$ defined as

$$
f(x,y)={x}^{3}\sqrt{y},
$$

the quadratic Taylor polynomial of $f$ about $a=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 1\end{aligned}]$ is given by

$$
f(x,y)≈f(a)+{f}^{′}(a)(x-a)+\frac{1}{2}{[\begin{aligned}∗ \\ y-1\end{aligned}]}^{T}[\begin{aligned}∗ & ∗ \\ 6 & -2\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}x-2 \\ y-1\end{aligned}].
$$

Find the sum of the three missing expressions.
questions.worked_solution:
Suppose that the function $f:{R}^{n}\to R$ is defined by 

$$
f:[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2} \\ ⋮ \\ {x}_{n}\end{aligned}]⟶z
$$

 

and is twice differentiable at $x=a.$ Then, the quadratic Taylor polynomial of $f$ about $a$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & ≈f(a)+{f}^{′}(a)(x-a)+\frac{1}{2}(x-a)^{T}{f}^{″}(a)(x-a),\end{aligned}
$$

where

$$
{f}^{′}(a)={[\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂{x}_{1}} & \frac{∂f}{∂{x}_{2}} & ⋯ & \frac{∂f}{∂{x}_{n}}\end{aligned}]|}_{x=a}
$$

and

$$
{f}^{″}(a)={[\begin{aligned}\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{1}^{2}} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{1}∂{x}_{2}} & ⋯ & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{1}∂{x}_{n}} \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{2}∂{x}_{1}} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{2}^{2}} & ⋯ & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{2}∂{x}_{n}} \\ ⋮ & ⋮ & ⋮ & ⋮ \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{n}∂{x}_{1}} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{n}∂{x}_{2}} & ⋯ & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{n}^{2}}\end{aligned}]}_{x=a}
$$

In this case, we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(x) & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & \frac{∂f}{∂y}\end{aligned}], & \,{f}^{″}(x) & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂x∂y} \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂y∂x} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{y}^{2}}\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Calculating the first derivative, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(x) & =[\begin{aligned}3{x}^{2}\sqrt{y} & \frac{{x}^{3}}{2\sqrt{y}}\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Calculating the second derivative, we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{″}(x) & =[\begin{aligned}6x\sqrt{y} & \frac{3{x}^{2}}{2\sqrt{y}} \\ \frac{3{x}^{2}}{2\sqrt{y}} & -\frac{{x}^{3}}{4\sqrt{{y}^{3}}}\end{aligned}] \\ {f}^{″}(2,1) & =[\begin{aligned}12 & 6 \\ 6 & -2\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the second-degree Taylor polynomial is given by

$$
f(x)≈f(a)+{f}^{′}(a)(x-a)+\frac{1}{2}{[\begin{aligned}x-2 \\ y-1\end{aligned}]}^{T}[\begin{aligned}12 & 6 \\ 6 & -2\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}x-2 \\ y-1\end{aligned}].
$$

Finally, the sum of the missing expressions is

$$
(x-2)+12+6=x+16.
$$

questions.problem:
For the twice-differentiable function $f:{R}^{3}\to R,$ we have the following data:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(1,0,1) & =2, & \,{f}^{′}(1,0,1) & =[\begin{aligned}2 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}], & \,{f}^{″}(1,0,1) & =[\begin{aligned}2 & 1 & -1 \\ 1 & 0 & 0 \\ -1 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Use the quadratic Taylor polynomial of $f$ about $a=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]$ to approximate the value of $f(0,1,1).$
questions.worked_solution:
Suppose that the function $f:{R}^{n}\to R$ is defined by 

$$
f:[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2} \\ ⋮ \\ {x}_{n}\end{aligned}]⟶z
$$

 

and is twice differentiable at $x=a.$ Then, the quadratic Taylor polynomial of $f$ about $a$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & ≈f(a)+{f}^{′}(a)(x-a)+\frac{1}{2}(x-a)^{T}{f}^{″}(a)(x-a),\end{aligned}
$$

where

$$
{f}^{′}(a)={[\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂{x}_{1}} & \frac{∂f}{∂{x}_{2}} & ⋯ & \frac{∂f}{∂{x}_{n}}\end{aligned}]|}_{x=a}
$$

and

$$
{f}^{″}(a)={[\begin{aligned}\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{1}^{2}} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{1}∂{x}_{2}} & ⋯ & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{1}∂{x}_{n}} \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{2}∂{x}_{1}} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{2}^{2}} & ⋯ & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{2}∂{x}_{n}} \\ ⋮ & ⋮ & ⋮ & ⋮ \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{n}∂{x}_{1}} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{n}∂{x}_{2}} & ⋯ & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{n}^{2}}\end{aligned}]}_{x=a}
$$

In this case, we have $a=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{aligned}],$ and the following data:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(a) & =2, & \,{f}^{′}(a) & =[\begin{aligned}2 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}], & \,{f}^{″}(a) & =[\begin{aligned}2 & 1 & -1 \\ 1 & 0 & 0 \\ -1 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the second-degree Taylor polynomial is given by

$$
f(x)≈2+[\begin{aligned}2 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}x-1 \\ y \\ z-1\end{aligned}]+\frac{1}{2}{[\begin{aligned}x-1 \\ y \\ z-1\end{aligned}]}^{T}[\begin{aligned}2 & 1 & -1 \\ 1 & 0 & 0 \\ -1 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}x-1 \\ y \\ z-1\end{aligned}]
$$

Finally, evaluating the polynomial at $x=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1 \\ 1\end{aligned}],$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(0,1,1) & ≈2+[\begin{aligned}2 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}0-1 \\ 1 \\ 1-1\end{aligned}]+\frac{1}{2}{[\begin{aligned}0-1 \\ 1 \\ 1-1\end{aligned}]}^{T}[\begin{aligned}2 & 1 & -1 \\ 1 & 0 & 0 \\ -1 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}0-1 \\ 1 \\ 1-1\end{aligned}] \\  & =2+[\begin{aligned}2 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]+\frac{1}{2}{[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]}^{T}[\begin{aligned}2 & 1 & -1 \\ 1 & 0 & 0 \\ -1 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{aligned}] \\  & =2+(-2)+\frac{1}{2}[\begin{aligned}-1 & 1 & 0\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}-1 \\ -1 \\ 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(0) \\  & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
For the twice-differentiable function $f:{R}^{3}\to R,$ we have the following data:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(\pi ,1,0) & =-1, & \,{f}^{′}(\pi ,1,0) & =[\begin{aligned}0 & 0 & 1+\pi \end{aligned}], & \,{f}^{″}(\pi ,1,0) & =[\begin{aligned}-1 & 1 & 0 \\ 1 & 1 & -1 \\ 0 & -1 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Use the quadratic Taylor polynomial of $f$ about $a=[\begin{aligned}\pi  \\ 1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]$ to approximate the value of $f(\pi ,0,1).$
questions.worked_solution:
Suppose that the function $f:{R}^{n}\to R$ is defined by 

$$
f:[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2} \\ ⋮ \\ {x}_{n}\end{aligned}]⟶z
$$

 

and is twice differentiable at $x=a.$ Then, the quadratic Taylor polynomial of $f$ about $a$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & ≈f(a)+{f}^{′}(a)(x-a)+\frac{1}{2}(x-a)^{T}{f}^{″}(a)(x-a),\end{aligned}
$$

where

$$
{f}^{′}(a)={[\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂{x}_{1}} & \frac{∂f}{∂{x}_{2}} & ⋯ & \frac{∂f}{∂{x}_{n}}\end{aligned}]|}_{x=a}
$$

and

$$
{f}^{″}(a)={[\begin{aligned}\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{1}^{2}} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{1}∂{x}_{2}} & ⋯ & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{1}∂{x}_{n}} \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{2}∂{x}_{1}} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{2}^{2}} & ⋯ & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{2}∂{x}_{n}} \\ ⋮ & ⋮ & ⋮ & ⋮ \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{n}∂{x}_{1}} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{n}∂{x}_{2}} & ⋯ & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{n}^{2}}\end{aligned}]}_{x=a}
$$

In this case, we have $a=[\begin{aligned}\pi  \\ 1 \\ 0\end{aligned}],$ and the following data:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(a) & =-1, & \,{f}^{′}(a) & =[\begin{aligned}0 & 0 & 1+\pi \end{aligned}], & \,{f}^{″}(a) & =[\begin{aligned}-1 & 1 & 0 \\ 1 & 1 & -1 \\ 0 & -1 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the second-degree Taylor polynomial is given by

$$
f(x)≈-1+[\begin{aligned}0 & 0 & 1+\pi \end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}x-\pi  \\ y-1 \\ z\end{aligned}]+\frac{1}{2}{[\begin{aligned}x-\pi  \\ y-1 \\ z\end{aligned}]}^{T}[\begin{aligned}-1 & 1 & 0 \\ 1 & 1 & -1 \\ 0 & -1 & 0\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}x-\pi  \\ y-1 \\ z\end{aligned}]
$$

Finally, evaluating the polynomial at $x=[\begin{aligned}\pi  \\ 0 \\ 1\end{aligned}],$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(\pi ,0,1) & ≈-1+[\begin{aligned}0 & 0 & 1+\pi \end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}\pi -\pi  \\ 0-1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]+\frac{1}{2}{[\begin{aligned}\pi -\pi  \\ 0-1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]}^{T}[\begin{aligned}-1 & 1 & 0 \\ 1 & 1 & -1 \\ 0 & -1 & 0\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}\pi -\pi  \\ 0-1 \\ 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =-1+[\begin{aligned}0 & 0 & 1+\pi \end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}0 \\ -1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]+\frac{1}{2}{[\begin{aligned}0 \\ -1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]}^{T}[\begin{aligned}-1 & 1 & 0 \\ 1 & 1 & -1 \\ 0 & -1 & 0\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}0 \\ -1 \\ 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =-1+1+\pi +\frac{1}{2}[\begin{aligned}0 & -1 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}-1 \\ -2 \\ 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =\pi +\frac{1}{2}(3) \\  & =\pi +\frac{3}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
For the twice-differentiable function $f:{R}^{3}\to R,$ we have the following data:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(1,1,0) & =1+e, & \,{f}^{′}(1,1,0) & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 & 2\end{aligned}], & \,{f}^{″}(1,1,0) & =[\begin{aligned}-1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & -1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 4\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

questions.worked_solution:
Suppose that the function $f:{R}^{n}\to R$ is defined by 

$$
f:[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2} \\ ⋮ \\ {x}_{n}\end{aligned}]⟶z
$$

$$

In this case, we have $a=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{aligned}],$ and the following data:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(a) & =1+e, & \,{f}^{′}(a) & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 & 2\end{aligned}], & \,{f}^{″}(a) & =[\begin{aligned}-1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & -1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 4\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the second-degree Taylor polynomial is given by

$$
f(x)≈1+e+[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 & 2\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}x-1 \\ y-1 \\ z\end{aligned}]+\frac{1}{2}{[\begin{aligned}x-1 \\ y-1 \\ z\end{aligned}]}^{T}[\begin{aligned}-1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & -1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 4\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}x-1 \\ y-1 \\ z\end{aligned}]

$$
\begin{aligned}f(2,2,2) & ≈1+e+[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 & 2\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}2-1 \\ 2-1 \\ 2\end{aligned}]+\frac{1}{2}{[\begin{aligned}2-1 \\ 2-1 \\ 2\end{aligned}]}^{T}[\begin{aligned}-1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & -1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 4\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}2-1 \\ 2-1 \\ 2\end{aligned}] \\  & =1+e+[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 & 2\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1 \\ 2\end{aligned}]+\frac{1}{2}{[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1 \\ 2\end{aligned}]}^{T}[\begin{aligned}-1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & -1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 4\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1 \\ 2\end{aligned}] \\  & =1+e+6+\frac{1}{2}[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 & 2\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}-1 \\ -1 \\ 8\end{aligned}] \\  & =7+e+\frac{1}{2}(14) \\  & =14+e.\end{aligned}
